texts: Aquinas is used for causation and dependence. Augustine contributes on grace; Athanasius supplies a historical New Testament list. Each use has a stated scope. None endorses every doctrine of its author or erases disagreements over justification, merit, canon or church authority.

Christian Scripture also confesses one God. Jesus commands baptism in the singular name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit; the comparison concerns how this confession fits together, rather than whether Christians worship three gods.
Read all four verses together. Distinguish the rejection of begetting from the Christian meaning of the eternal Son; ask what your neighbour thinks Christians mean.

These readings serve a Christian conversation about trusting Jesus: understand God’s identity, examine Jesus’ identity, consider forgiveness through his death and resurrection, then assess the claims of revelation. Read each Qur’anic passage on its own terms beside the Christian counterpart. Ask what your neighbour believes and why; the sequence guides discussion rather than guaranteeing conversion.

texts: Both start from God’s oneness, which they get right, and then try to find threeness by dividing the one thing up — into states, stages, functions or aspects. Division is the only tool they have. But a divided unity is not three persons; it is one thing described three ways. So the threeness always comes out thinner than the oneness, and what is lost is precisely what Scripture shows: three who speak to each other, send each other, glorify each other and love each other, eternally and at once.

Ice, water and steam becomes modalism at one specific moment: when someone says “so that is what God is like” and stops. Said with its limit attached — “this will show you one substance and will tell you nothing whatever about three persons; do not push it further” — even a poor picture can do a small honest job. The difference between an illustration and a false doctrine is, quite literally, the disclaimer.

Look at what the picture actually offers. Ice, liquid water and steam are not three things. They are three states of one thing. The hydrogen and oxygen are not aware of one another, do not address one another, and do not stand in any relation to one another; there is nothing there but one substance in one condition at a time. Put a given quantity of water in the freezer and it is ice; boil it and it is steam. It passes from state to state. It is never, as itself, all three.

Map that onto God and you get exactly Sabellius’s teaching: a single divine person who was Father under the old covenant, became Son for the span of a human life, and has been Spirit since Pentecost. Three successive appearances of one actor. On that account the Father never sends the Son, because there is nobody to send and nobody to be sent; the Son never prays to the Father, because there is nobody to pray to; and the words “this is My beloved Son” are God talking about himself in the third person.

The Latin word the creeds use, persona, originally meant an actor’s mask. That is precisely the meaning the church rejected when it adopted the word. Sabellius’s God wears three masks; the creeds’ God is three persons. The analogy of the man with three jobs is not a rough approximation of the doctrine — it is a tidy statement of the position the doctrine was written to rule out. Roles are temporary, partial and relative to an audience; the Son is not a role the Father takes on, and did not begin at Bethlehem.

The second picture looks more promising, because at least it is about a person. That is exactly why it fails harder. A man who is a surgeon, a husband and a father is one person throughout. He has one mind, one will, one memory, one centre from which he acts. “Surgeon” and “father” are not someone; they are descriptions of how this someone stands to other people.

texts: And the catholic faith is this: that we worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity; neither confounding the Persons, nor dividing the Essence.

That is the sentence most often quoted in English as “neither confounding the Persons, nor dividing the Substance” — the wording of the Book of Common Prayer. Both render the same Latin, substantiam separantes; this site’s copy of the creed translates substantia as “Essence”, which is why the words above read that way. The creed then spells out what it has just forbidden, clause by clause: the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God, “and yet they are not three Gods; but one God”, and “the whole three Persons are coeternal, and coequal”.

The distinction between ousia and hupostasis is the same as that between the general and the particular; as, for instance, between the animal and the particular man. Wherefore, in the case of the Godhead, we confess one essence or substance so as not to give a variant definition of existence, but we confess a particular hypostasis, in order that our conception of Father, Son and Holy Spirit may be without confusion and clear.

What Scripture says of the Spirit in relation to the Father (John 15:26), and only of the Spirit. The Athanasian Creed is deliberate that this is “neither made, nor created, nor begotten; but proceeding”.

With those words in place, the shortest full statement in the Christian tradition can be made in a line. The Athanasian Creed — Latin, and certainly not written by Athanasius, whatever its name says; scholars place its composition in the fifth or sixth century, and this site’s collection dates the received text at about 800 — fences the doctrine on both sides at once:

“In the name” is singular — one name, not three. And three are named inside it, each with its own article in the Greek, each distinguished from the others. Baptism, the act by which a person is handed over to God, is performed into a single name that has three persons in it. This is not a later theological construction laid over the text; it is the text the construction had to account for.

texts: A presbyter of Alexandria named Arius gave the second answer, carefully and in writing. His case was not stupid, which is why it took sixty years to settle. If the Son is begotten, he argued, then there was a point from which he is; if he is from the Father, then the Father is the source and the Son is not; and whatever is not the source is, in the end, among the things that came to be. So the Son is the first and greatest of all creatures, made before time, through whom everything else was made — but not God as the Father is God. The slogan the council later quoted back at his party was “there was a time when he was not”.

And we believe in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and Giver of Life; who proceeds from the Father and the Son; who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified; who spoke by the prophets.

But the tri-personality of God is not a numerical or essential trinity of three beings (like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob), for this would be tritheism; nor is it, on the other hand, merely a threefold aspect and mode of manifestation, in the Sabellian or Swedenborgian sense; but it is a real, objective, and eternal, though ineffable, distinction in the one Divine being

Each person is a third of God; you need all three to make a deity. It loses both at once — no person is fully God, and the one God is an assembly. “Partialism” is a modern teaching label and not a word any council used, which is worth saying plainly. But the thing it names was refused at Nicaea in as many words: the Son is of the Father and yet “does not subsist as a part of the Father”, and not by “division or abscission”.

Look at what the clause does. It does not say the Spirit is homoousios — the council avoided repeating the word that had caused sixty years of trouble. It says something harder to argue with: the Spirit is worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son. Whatever may be worshipped is God; the church worships the Spirit; therefore. And it calls the Spirit “the Lord and Giver of Life”, which is not language that can be used of a creature.

Paired with it is the phrase that is still recited every Sunday: begotten, not made. Arius’s whole case rested on treating “begotten” as a soft word for “made”. The creed separates them permanently. Begetting is a relation inside God; making is what God does to things that are not God.

Read the creed of 325 again and notice how it ends. “[We believe] also in the Holy Spirit.” That is the whole of it. One clause, no description, nothing about what the Spirit is or how the Spirit stands to the Father and the Son. The council had been called about the Son, and about the Son it was exhaustive; on the Spirit it said the minimum.

So the same argument came round again, one person later. If the Son is God, is the Spirit? A party in the following generation said no — that the Spirit is a created power, a servant, the greatest of ministering beings. Their opponents called them Pneumatomachi, the Spirit-fighters; in the historical narratives of the period they appear under the name Macedonians, after Macedonius of Constantinople. Their leaders were invited to the next council and walked out of it.

The English copy quoted above reads “who proceeds from the Father and the Son”. The two added words are the Filioque — Latin for “and the Son” — and they are a later Western addition, not part of what the hundred and fifty bishops wrote. They spread through the Latin church over the following centuries and became one of the standing causes of the division between East and West in 1054. Schaff’s own edition on this site brackets them, “[and the Son]”, to mark them as an interpolation; the Latin text of 381 above has only ex Patre procedentem, from the Father. If you are reading the creed to find out what 381 said, read the clause without them.

The appeal of this is that it keeps the arithmetic simple. There is one God, the Father; the Son is an exalted creature; nothing needs to be said about three being one. The price is the entire worshipping practice of the church, which was already praying to Jesus, baptising into his name alongside the Father’s, and calling him Lord in the sense Israel reserved for God.

Three Gods of the same kind, like three men — the error Gregory of Nyssa was accused of and spent a whole treatise answering. It keeps the three and loses the one. No council legislated against it by that name, because nobody taught it on purpose; it is where the other repairs land when you push them. Schaff names it in a single sentence beside Sabellianism, below.

We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of all things visible and invisible:—and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the only-begotten of the Father, that is of the substance of the Father; God of God, Light of light, true God of true God; begotten not made, consubstantial with the Father; by whom all things were made both which are in heaven and on earth; who for the sake of us men, and on account of our salvation, descended, became incarnate, was made man, suffered and rose again on the third day; he ascended into the heavens, and will come to judge the living and the dead. [We believe] also in the Holy Spirit.

Which brings this article back where part three left it. The councils tell you what cannot be said. They do not give you a picture, and they never claimed to. Nicaea does not explain how the Son is of one being with the Father; it rules out the explanations that fail. Constantinople does not explain the procession of the Spirit; it says the Spirit is worshipped with the Father and the Son, and leaves it there.

with the insertion, however, of that single word “homoousios” (consubstantial), an expression which the emperor himself explained, as not indicating corporeal affections or properties; and consequently that the Son did not subsist from the Father either by division or abscission

texts: “Not by division or abscission.” “Not as a part of the Father.” In the same session in which the church affirmed that the Son is of one being with the Father, it denied that he is a slice of the Father — which is exactly what the water analogy and the three-sided figures suggest, and exactly what the modern label “partialism” names. The council saw that danger in the word it was adopting, and fenced it in advance.

“Real, objective, and eternal, though ineffable.” Each of those four words is load-bearing. Real and objective, against modalism: the distinction is in God and not in our perception of God. Eternal, against Arianism: it did not begin. Ineffable, against every diagram in this article, including the good ones.

texts: But in the case of the Divine nature we do not similarly learn that the Father does anything by Himself in which the Son does not work conjointly, or again that the Son has any special operation apart from the Holy Spirit; but every operation which extends from God to the Creation, and is named according to our variable conceptions of it, has its origin from the Father, and proceeds through the Son, and is perfected in the Holy Spirit.

Count, if you must; but you must not by counting do damage to the faith. … For we do not count by way of addition, gradually making increase from unity to multitude, and saying one, two, and three,—nor yet first, second, and third. For “I,” God, “am the first, and I am the last.”

Directing my purpose by this rule of faith, so far as I have been able, so far as Thou hast made me to be able, I have sought Thee, and have desired to see with my understanding what I believed; and I have argued and labored much. … May I remember Thee, understand Thee, love Thee. Increase these things in me, until Thou renewest me wholly. … O Lord the one God, God the Trinity, whatever I have said in these books that is of Thine, may they acknowledge who are Thine; if anything of my own, may it be pardoned both by Thee and by those who are Thine. Amen.

Earlier in the work he had already said why no vocabulary was going to be adequate. The famous sentence is not a flourish; it is an admission of defeat about language, offered in defence of using the words anyway.

Gregory’s first move is unexpected: he does not defend the analogy, he attacks the ordinary speech on which it rests. Strictly, he says, “three men” is sloppy. Human nature is one; what there are three of is persons bearing it. We call them three men out of habit, not accuracy.

I picture to myself an eye, a fountain, a river, as others have done before, to see if the first might be analogous to the Father, the second to the Son, and the third to the Holy Ghost. … But I was afraid in the first place that I should present a flow in the Godhead, incapable of standing still; and secondly that by this figure a numerical unity would be introduced. For the eye and the spring and the river are numerically one, though in different forms.

In a word, there is nothing which presents a standing point to my mind in these illustrations from which to consider the Object which I am trying to represent to myself, unless one may indulgently accept one point of the image while rejecting the rest. Finally, then, it seems best to me to let the images and the shadows go, as being deceitful and very far short of the truth; and clinging myself to the more reverent conception, and resting upon few words, using the guidance of the Holy Ghost …

In his last book Augustine returns to his own analogies and takes them apart. The likeness of memory to the Father, he says, is “incomparably unequal, yet of some sort, whatever it be”; the likeness of understanding to the Son holds only “in its own great disparity”; the likeness of love to the Spirit is “some, however exceedingly unequal, likeness of the Holy Spirit”. And then he names the break that cannot be repaired by any refinement: the three in a human mind are not three persons but one, while in God they are three persons and one God. The image is an image of the Trinity; it is not a small Trinity.

In the second way, reasons avail to prove the Trinity; as, when assumed to be true, such reasons confirm it. We must not, however, think that the trinity of persons is adequately proved by such reasons.

Lewis builds his picture out of dimensions. In one dimension you can only have a line. In two, lines combine into a figure — a square is made of four lines without ceasing to be one square. In three, figures combine into a solid — a cube is made of six squares without ceasing to be one cube. At each level the simpler thing is not abandoned but taken up: you do not stop having lines when you start having squares. His suggestion is that the same relation holds between human personality and God’s: on our level, one being means one person, and that remains true of us; on God’s level, one being is three persons, in a way that includes rather than contradicts what personality means down here.

Since, then, these three, memory, understanding, will, are not three lives, but one life; nor three minds, but one mind; it follows certainly that neither are they three substances, but one substance.

The attraction of this is that it finds threeness inside something that is obviously one. One act of love is not one thing; it necessarily has a structure of three. You cannot subtract the beloved and still have love, or subtract the love and still have a lover. Each requires the other two, and what you have is not three loves but one. For a doctrine that needs distinction without division, that is a real gain on anything the water or the three jobs can offer.

This is the most useful thing in Lewis’s chapter, and it is not an analogy at all. It is a description of what Christians think is actually happening when they pray — which is why it does not break the way the illustrations do. The doctrine is not being compared to something; it is being located in an ordinary evening.

Two processions, and only two, because a mind has only these two kinds of inner act: knowing and loving. The procession of the Word is called generation, and so the Word is the Son; the procession of love is not generation, and so has no comparable name — the tradition calls it spiration, and the one who proceeds is the Holy Spirit. This is why the creeds are careful that the Son is “begotten” and the Spirit “proceeding”, and refuse to use the one word for the other.

texts: A Persian royal city: the setting of Esther and of Nehemiah's service. Esther 1:2; Nehemiah 1:1.
A lame man healed; Paul stoned and left for dead. Acts 14:8–20.
A port city where Paul stayed eighteen months; two of his letters answer its church. Acts 18:1–11.
Abraham was sent to the land of Moriah with Isaac; Solomon built the temple on Mount Moriah. Genesis 22:2; 2 Chronicles 3:1.
Abraham's home by the oaks of Mamre, and David's first capital. Genesis 13:18; 2 Samuel 2:1–4.
Abram built an altar between Bethel and Ai, and came back to it from Egypt. Genesis 12:8; 13:3.
Abram went down to Egypt in a famine; Genesis names no city, so the dot marks the land. Genesis 12:10.
After the shipwreck all 276 on board reached land, and Paul healed the sick of the island. Acts 27:37, 44; 28:1–9.
An ancient capital of Egypt, named by the prophets. Jeremiah 46:14; Hosea 9:6.
Burned by Nebuchadnezzar's army; the people taken to Babylon. 2 Kings 25:8–11.
By the rivers of Babylon the exiles wept for Zion. Psalm 137:1; Daniel 1:1–6.
Capital of Aram, whose king Rezin waged war against Jerusalem. Isaiah 7:8; 2 Kings 16:5.
Capital of Assyria, whose judgment Nahum announced. Nahum 1:1; 3:7.
Capital of Assyria; Sennacherib returned here from Judah. 2 Kings 19:36.
Capital of the empire that carried Judah into exile. 2 Kings 25:8–11; Daniel 1:1–2.
Capital of the empire. Paul wrote to its church, then reached it under guard. Romans 1:7; Acts 28:14–16.
Cornelius heard the gospel here, and Paul was held two years. Acts 10:1, 24–48; 24:27.
Egypt's great harbour; an Alexandrian ship carried Paul toward Italy. Acts 27:6.
Faithful in suffering: “Be faithful even unto death.” Revelation 2:8–11.
Fell to Assyria; Israel was carried away and settled in Halah, in Gozan by the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes. 2 Kings 17:5–6.
Israel set out from Rameses. Exodus 12:37; Numbers 33:3.
Jacob saw the stairway to heaven on the way out, and built an altar here on the way home. Genesis 28:10–19; 35:1–7.
Jacob served Laban twenty years: fourteen for his two daughters, six for the flocks. Genesis 29:4; 31:41.
Jesus' home by the Sea of Galilee. Matthew 4:13; Mark 2:1.
Jonah found a ship for Tarshish here; Peter saw the vision of the sheet on a rooftop. Jonah 1:3; Acts 10:9–16.
Many stations on this route are traditional locations; scholars place several of them differently.
Paul warned that the voyage would end in disaster; the centurion sailed on. Acts 27:8–11.
Paul's home city in Cilicia. Acts 21:39; 22:3.

Peter's confession: “You are the Christ.” Matthew 16:13–16.
Taken from Shiloh into battle, captured by the Philistines, sent back, and brought up to Jerusalem by David. 1 Samuel 4–7; 2 Samuel 6.

The city of David and of the temple, where Jesus was crucified and rose. 2 Samuel 5:6–7; Luke 24:1–7.

The tabernacle's home in the days of the judges and of Samuel. Joshua 18:1; 1 Samuel 1:3.
Town of Ruth and David, and the birthplace of Jesus. Ruth 1:19; Micah 5:2; Luke 2:4–7.
Where Jesus grew up, and where his own town rejected him. Luke 2:51; 4:16–30.
